title: The Reservation Inflation of Hard Money: Gold-Standard Deflation and the Real Expansion of Nominal Claims, 1873-1896
summary: This paper extends the Store of Value Circulation Reserve (SCR) theory of inflation by examining whether reservation inflation—the real appreciation of nominal claims relative to goods—can arise during a hard-money era when circulation inflation (CPI) is negative. Using British retail price data and U.S. historical CPI, the author finds that between 1873-1896, while prices fell from 18.0 to 14.7 in Britain and 36.0 to 25.0 in the U.S., a fixed-claim reservation index rose 22.4% in Britain and 44.0% in the U.S. The paper argues hard money does not eliminate inflationary pressure but relocates it from consumer prices to nominal claim values.
key_points: Britain's price index fell from 18.0 (1873) to 14.7 (1896), a decline of approximately 18%
U.S. historical CPI fell from 36.0 (1873) to 25.0 (1896), a decline of approximately 31%
Despite negative circulation inflation, Britain's fixed-claim reservation index rose 22.4%
U.S. fixed-claim reservation index rose 44.0%, mechanically increasing the real burden of fixed nominal claims
Author Ran Huang (single author) tests the SCR theory's second proposition about reservation inflation under monetary constraint
Paper is positioned as a companion to a prior Japan study on monetary-base expansion under reserve-dominant phases
why_it_matters: This historical case study challenges simplistic hard-money narratives by showing that gold-standard deflation did not eliminate inflationary pressure but transformed its expression from consumer prices to nominal claim values. The findings suggest CPI alone may understate monetary-material asymmetry during reserve-dominant regimes.
